unit.title: Japanese candlesticks
unit.description: Reading each candle, the main patterns and how well they really work

steps.title: From rice to your screen
steps.body: Candlesticks were born in the **Dojima** rice market (Osaka, eighteenth century); tradition credits the merchant Munehisa Homma with them. They reached the West with **Steve Nison**'s book in 1991 and today they're the default chart on almost every platform.

steps.title: The parts
steps.body:
• **Body:** between the open and the close.
• **Upper wick:** from the body to the **high**.
• **Lower wick:** from the body to the **low**.

**Green:** closes above the open. **Red:** closes below it. In China, Japan and Korea the colours are usually the other way round: check the legend.

steps.title: An example with numbers
steps.body: Candle with O = 100, H = 108, L = 97, C = 106: it's green (106 > 100), its body measures 6 (from 100 to 106), the upper wick 2 (from 106 to 108), the lower wick 3 (from 97 to 100) and the total range 11.
steps.key: The body runs from the open to the close; the wicks reach the high and the low.
steps.tip: Green: the close is at the top. Red: the close is at the bottom.

steps.title: The body: conviction
steps.body:
• **Long green body:** buyers dominated from start to finish.
• **Long red body:** sellers dominated.
• **Small body:** indecision.

«Long» is always relative to the previous candles: €2 is a lot for a quiet share and nothing for a crypto.

steps.title: The wicks: rejection
steps.body:
• **Long upper wick:** the price went up, but sellers pushed it back down. Rejection of higher prices.
• **Long lower wick:** it fell, but buyers pushed it back up. Rejection of lower prices.

steps.prompt: Tap the candle that tells this story: «sellers sank it and buyers pushed it back almost to the top»
steps.ok: That long lower wick is the rejection of lower prices. After several falls, this is what a hammer looks like.
steps.ko: Look for the longest thin line below a small body.

steps.title: Location is everything
steps.body: The same candle means different things depending on where it appears: after a long fall and at a support level it can signal that sellers are exhausted; in the middle of a range, almost nothing.
steps.key: A big body is conviction; a long wick is a rejection.
steps.tip: Don't read a candle on its own: ask yourself where the price has come from.

steps.title: Marubozu: strength
steps.body:
A long body with little or no wick (*marubozu* means «shaven head» in Japanese).

• **Bullish:** opens at the low and closes at the high.
• **Bearish:** opens at the high and closes at the low.

It usually signals that the strength will continue, especially at the start of a move or when a level breaks.

steps.title: Spinning top and doji: doubt and a draw
steps.body:
• **Spinning top:** small body with similar wicks above and below. Indecision.
• **Doji:** open and close almost the same; the body is just a line.

Types of doji: **standard** (cross), **long-legged**, **dragonfly** (T shape, long lower wick) and **gravestone** (upside-down T, long upper wick).

steps.prompt: Tap the doji: the candle where the open and close almost match
steps.ok: Almost no body and wicks on both sides: neither buyers nor sellers won that session.
steps.ko: Look for the candle whose body is almost just a line.

steps.title: What the data says
steps.body: According to Bulkowski, the dragonfly doji acts as a reversal only **half the time**: like tossing a coin. A doji is a signal to pay attention, not to act.
steps.key: Marubozu means strength; spinning top, doubt; doji, a draw.
steps.tip: A doji doesn't say «it's going to reverse». It says «nobody knows what to do». Wait for the next candle.

steps.title: The rule and the four names
steps.body:
A **small** body at one end, a wick at least **2–3 times** the size of the body and little wick on the other side. The name depends on where it appears:

• Long lower wick after a **fall**: **hammer**.
• The same, after a **rise**: **hanging man**.
• Long upper wick after a **fall**: **inverted hammer**.
• The same, after a **rise**: **shooting star**.

steps.prompt: After the rise, tap the shooting star
steps.ok: Small body at the bottom and a long upper wick: buyers had a go and sellers pushed it back down.
steps.ko: Look for the longest upper wick after several rising candles.

steps.title: What the data says (Bulkowski)
steps.body:
• Hammer: reverses upwards **60 %** of the time (rank 65 of 103).
• Hanging man: keeps rising **59 %** of the time! (rank 87).
• Shooting star: reverses downwards **59 %** of the time (rank 55).

He himself describes them as «not far from random».
steps.key: The same shape changes its name depending on whether it comes after a rise or a fall.
steps.tip: A hammer is only a hammer after a fall. And even then, without context it's barely better than a coin.

steps.title: Engulfing patterns
steps.body:
**Bullish:** after a fall, a red candle followed by a green one that opens below the previous close and **closes above its open**. Its body swallows the red one.

**Bearish:** after a rise, a green candle followed by a red one whose body engulfs the green one.

steps.title: Harami, piercing pattern and dark cloud cover
steps.body:
• **Harami** («pregnant»): a long candle followed by a small one **inside** its body. The momentum stalls.
• **Piercing pattern:** after a fall, a green candle that closes **above the midpoint** of the previous red body.
• **Dark cloud cover:** after a rise, a red candle that closes **below the midpoint** of the green one.

steps.prompt: Tap the green candle that engulfs the previous red one
steps.ok: Its body completely swallows the previous day's red one: buyers won back everything that was lost and more.
steps.ko: Look for a huge green candle straight after a red one.

steps.title: The data paradox
steps.body: Bulkowski: the bullish engulfing reverses **63 %** of the time (rank 84 of 103); the bearish one, **79 %**, but it ranks only **91** because the move that follows is usually small. Dark cloud cover reverses **60 %** of the time (rank 22).
steps.key: Getting the direction right isn't enough: the size of the move has to make up for the risk.
steps.tip: An engulfing pattern often reverses, but sometimes not by much.

steps.title: Morning star and evening star
steps.body:
**Morning** (bullish reversal): after a fall, a long red candle, a small candle that gaps down (the «star») and a long green candle that closes at least **halfway** up the body of the first.

**Evening** (bearish reversal): the same in reverse, after a rise. If the middle one is a doji, they're called doji stars.

steps.title: Soldiers and crows
steps.body:
• **Three white soldiers:** three long green candles in a row, each closing higher and near its high.
• **Three black crows:** three long red candles after a rise, each closing near its low and making new lows.

steps.prompt: Tap the third candle of the morning star: the green one that confirms it
steps.ok: Long red candle, small candle of doubt and long green candle that wins back ground: a morning star.
steps.ko: Look for the sequence big red → small candle → big green, and tap the green one.

steps.title: The best numbers (Bulkowski)
steps.body:
• Morning star: reverses **78 %** of the time (rank 12 of 103).
• Evening star: **72 %** (rank **4**).
• Three white soldiers: **82 %** (rank 32).
• Three black crows: **78 %** (rank **3**).

Better than single candles, but much less common.
steps.key: Three candles tell the story better than one.
steps.tip: That's why they're more reliable… and rarer.

steps.title: The four filters
steps.body:
1. **Prior trend:** a reversal pattern needs something to reverse.
2. **Level:** support, resistance, a key moving average, or the year's low or high.
3. **Volume:** the higher it is above average, the more credible.
4. **Confirmation:** the next candle closes in the expected direction.

And daily or weekly charts are better than minute charts.

steps.prompt: Tap the hammer and then look at the next two candles
steps.ok: That's the hammer. The next candle closed above its high (confirmation)… and the one after fell sharply. Confirmation reduces mistakes; it doesn't eliminate them.
steps.ko: Look for the longest lower wick after the fall.

steps.title: What the research says
steps.body:
• **Marshall, Young and Rose** tested 28 patterns on Dow Jones shares (1992–2002): they added no value. A study in Japan (1975–2004), the birthplace of candlesticks, reached the same conclusion.
• Bulkowski measures without commissions or *spreads*.
• If you test a hundred patterns, some will seem to work by pure chance (*data snooping*).

steps.title: So what are they good for?
steps.body: For reading the market (rejection, conviction, indecision), for putting your stop in a logical place and for not being fooled by people selling patterns «with a 90 % success rate».
steps.key: Candlesticks are a language, not a crystal ball.
steps.tip: The candle is the sentence; the context is the whole book.

u20l1-1.prompt: On a green candle, match each point with its price.
u20l1-1.explanation: On a green candle the open is at the bottom and the close at the top; on a red one, the other way round. The wicks always reach the high and the low.

u20l1-2.prompt: Candle with an open of 40, high of 44, low of 39 and close of 43. What colour is it?
u20l1-2.explanation: It closes (43) above the open (40): it's bullish, green.

u20l1-3.prompt: Candle with an open of 40, high of 44, low of 39 and close of 43. How big is the body?
u20l1-3.explanation: From the open at 40 to the close at 43: 3 points.

u20l1-4.prompt: Green candle with an open of 40, high of 44, low of 39 and close of 43. How long is its lower wick?
u20l1-4.explanation: From the open (40), which is the bottom of the body, to the low (39): 1 point.

u20l1-5.prompt: Red candle with an open of 62, high of 63, low of 55 and close of 57. How big is its body?
u20l1-5.explanation: From 62 to 57: 5 points. On a red candle, the open is at the top and the close at the bottom.

u20l1-6.prompt: On a red candle, the open is at the ____ of the body.
u20l1-6.explanation: If it closes below the open, the open ends up at the top and the close at the bottom.

u20l1-7.prompt: Tap the candle with the longest lower wick.
u20l1-7.explanation: The price fell a long way during that session, but recovered before the close. That thin line is the path down to the low. (Amazon · daily candles · February 2025)

u20l1-8.prompt: Put the prices of a green candle with wicks in order from lowest to highest.
u20l1-8.explanation: Low ≤ open < close ≤ high. On a red candle, the open and close swap places.

u20l1-9.prompt: On every platform in the world, green means the price went up.
u20l1-9.explanation: In China, Japan and Korea the colours are usually the other way round: red for up and green for down.

u20l1-10.prompt: The book that brought Japanese candlesticks to the West in 1991 was written by Steve ____.
u20l1-10.explanation: Steve Nison published Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques in 1991.

u20l2-1.prompt: What does a very long upper wick indicate?
options: That buyers dominated the whole period
u20l2-1.explanation: The price got up there, but sellers pushed it back down before the close.

options: Long red candle closing at the low
Opens at 50, falls to 44 and closes at 50.5
Opens at 30, rises to 34 and closes at 29
Long green candle, almost no wicks
u20l2-2.explanation: What matters is where it closes relative to the open and how much body it leaves. The wicks tell you about the failed attempts.

u20l2-3.prompt: Tap the candle where sellers won most clearly: the biggest red body.
u20l2-3.explanation: It opened high and closed almost at the low, with hardly any wicks: sellers were in charge the whole session. (NVIDIA · daily candles · December 2024 – January 2025)

u20l2-4.prompt: Now look for rejection of higher prices: tap the candle with the longest upper wick.
u20l2-4.explanation: Buyers drove the price a long way up, but the session closed well below that high. (Microsoft · daily candles · April 2026)

u20l2-5.prompt: A candle opens at 50, drops to 44 and closes at 50.5. How far did it fall from the open, in percentage terms?
u20l2-5.explanation: (50 − 44) ÷ 50 = 0.12 → −12 %. And even so it closed above the open: buyers won the battle.

u20l2-6.prompt: A candle with a €2 body is always a big candle.
u20l2-6.explanation: It depends on the asset and the previous candles: €2 is huge on a €20 share and almost nothing on a €500 one.

u20l2-7.prompt: Read the last few candles as a battle. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u20l2-7.explanation: Knowing who won each session doesn't tell you who'll win the next one. Candles describe; they don't predict.

u20l2-8.prompt: You see a candle with a very long lower wick in the middle of a sideways range, with no prior trend. Laura says it's a crystal-clear buy signal. What do you tell her?
options: That location matters: in the middle of a range, that candle says little
That she's right: long wick, safe buy
u20l2-8.explanation: A candle has to be read in context: where the price has come from and where it is now.
feedback: Exactly: the same candle after a long fall and at a support level would tell a different story.
The lower wick is a rejection of lower prices: it's not a sell signal, but here it's not a buy signal either.
In the middle of a range, with no trend to reverse, that wick means very little.

u20l2-9.prompt: Quick: a very small body means…
u20l2-9.explanation: Neither buyers nor sellers won clearly.

u20l2-10.prompt: How do you explain to Lumi what happened?
options: The candle has a long upper wick: higher prices were rejected
It was a great day for buyers
It's a bug in the app
u20l2-10.explanation: The high tells you how far buyers got; the close, who won.
feedback: That's it! Buyers got a long way, but sellers won the end of the battle.
Mid-morning, yes, but by the close sellers had pushed the price back down. Look at the close, not the high.
There's no bug: going up and coming back down is very normal, and the candle records it with the wick.
lines: My share went up 5 % this morning 🚀
But it closed almost at the opening price 😕

u20l3-1.prompt: Match each candle with the story it tells.
u20l3-1.explanation: The size of the body tells you about conviction; the wicks, about each side's attempts.
right: Indecision with movement in both directions
A draw: open and close almost the same
Sellers were in charge the whole session
Buyers were in charge the whole session

u20l3-2.prompt: Match each doji with its shape.
u20l3-2.explanation: In the dragonfly, buyers pushed the price right back to the top; in the gravestone, sellers pushed it back down.
right: Very long wicks on both sides
T shape: long lower wick, no upper wick

u20l3-3.prompt: Tap the doji on this chart.
u20l3-3.explanation: Open and close almost identical: the body is just a line. A draw in that session. (NVIDIA · daily candles · September 2026)

u20l3-4.prompt: Tap the marubozu: the green candle with a big body and almost no wicks.
u20l3-4.explanation: It opened practically at the low and closed at the high: buyers controlled the whole session. (Microsoft · daily candles · May–June 2026)

u20l3-5.prompt: Quick: open 25.10 and close 25.11, with wicks on both sides. Which candle is it?
u20l3-5.explanation: Open and close almost the same: a doji.

u20l3-6.prompt: A bullish marubozu opens at the high and closes at the low.
u20l3-6.explanation: The other way round: it opens at the low and closes at the high.

u20l3-7.prompt: According to Bulkowski, the dragonfly doji calls the reversal correctly 9 times out of 10.
u20l3-7.explanation: Only half the time, like a coin. That's why it's a signal to pay attention, not to act.

u20l3-8.prompt: The doji shaped like an upside-down T, with a long upper wick, is called a ____ doji.
u20l3-8.explanation: Buyers pushed the price up, but sellers pushed it right back down to the bottom.

u20l3-9.prompt: After three weeks of rises, a doji appears. Ana wants to sell everything because «the doji signals the reversal». What do you tell her?
options: To buy more: the doji is bullish
To wait for the next candle to see who wins
u20l3-9.explanation: A doji calls for attention and confirmation, not an immediate decision.
feedback: A doji only signals a draw. After a long rise it deserves attention, but without confirmation it's little better than a coin toss.
A doji has no direction: it's indecision.
Good: if the next candle closes sharply lower, the doji becomes more significant; if not, it was just a pause.

u20l3-10.explanation: Big body with no wicks = strength. Small or non-existent body = doubt or a draw.

u20l4-1.prompt: After the fall, tap the hammer.
u20l4-1.explanation: Small body at the top and a very long lower wick after several red candles: sellers pushed down and buyers pushed the price back up. (NVIDIA · daily candles · June 2026)

u20l4-2.prompt: After the rise, tap the shooting star.
u20l4-2.explanation: Upper wick several times bigger than the body: the attempt to go higher was rejected. (Amazon · daily candles · October–November 2025)

u20l4-3.prompt: Name each candle based on its shape and its context.
options: Small body at the top and long lower wick at a several-week low
Long upper wick after a fall
Long lower wick after a rise
Long lower wick after a fall
Long upper wick after a rise
u20l4-3.explanation: First the shape (where the long wick is) and then the context (where the price has come from).

u20l4-4.prompt: Where does the logical stop go if you buy after a confirmed hammer?
u20l4-4.explanation: If the price breaks below the low of the wick, the idea that lower prices were rejected has failed.

u20l4-5.prompt: A hammer has a high of €52 and a low of €47. You buy at €52 after confirmation and put your stop at €46.50. How much are you risking per share?
u20l4-5.explanation: 52 − 46.50 = €5.50 per share. The stop goes a little below the wick so it isn't triggered by a mere wick.

u20l4-6.prompt: According to Bulkowski, after a hanging man the price keeps rising more often than it reverses.
u20l4-6.explanation: Upward continuation 59 % of the time: the opposite of what classic theory says.

u20l4-7.prompt: Look at the wicks on the last few candles. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u20l4-7.explanation: Hammers and shooting stars reverse around 60 % of the time according to Bulkowski: slightly better than a coin, a long way from a certainty.

u20l4-8.prompt: You see a textbook hammer on a daily chart, after two weeks of falls and near the low for the year. Based on what you've learnt, what do you do?
options: I wait for confirmation and, if I go in, I put the stop below the wick
I ignore it: candlesticks are useless
I buy now with everything I've got
u20l4-8.explanation: A hammer is a clue, not an order: confirmation, a stop and a cautious position size.
feedback: Good: confirmation (a close above the hammer's high) and a stop where the idea no longer holds.
Candlesticks don't predict on their own, but they give you context and a logical place for the stop.
Even in good conditions it often fails: going all in without a stop turns a 60 % chance into roulette.

u20l4-9.prompt: Quick: long upper wick after a rise.
u20l4-9.explanation: Small body at the bottom and a long upper wick after a rise: shooting star.

u20l4-10.prompt: According to Bulkowski, what improves the hammer's results?
options: Appearing in the middle of a range
Appearing near the low for the year
u20l4-10.explanation: It works better in the lower third of the yearly range, and ones with a green body do better.

u20l5-1.prompt: After the rise, tap the red candle that engulfs the previous green one.
u20l5-1.explanation: The red body swallows the previous green one: sellers wipe out everything gained in the previous session. (Apple · daily candles · August–September 2026)

u20l5-2.prompt: Tap the bullish engulfing pattern on this chart.
u20l5-2.explanation: A green candle whose body completely covers the previous red one's, after several weak sessions. (NVIDIA · daily candles · July 2026)

u20l5-3.prompt: In a harami, the second candle…
options: Sits inside the first one's body
u20l5-3.explanation: It's the opposite of an engulfing pattern: a small candle inside the big one shows the momentum is stalling.

u20l5-4.prompt: Match each two-candle pattern with its story.
u20l5-4.explanation: Engulfing is a full counter-attack; the piercing pattern and dark cloud cover, a partial one; the harami, a pause.
right: Small candle inside the big one: the momentum stalls
After a rise, sellers wipe out more than half a green candle
After a fall, buyers win back more than half a red candle
Buyers win back all of yesterday's losses and more

u20l5-5.prompt: The bearish engulfing reverses 79 % of the time, but ranks only 91 of 103 for performance. Why?
options: Because it only works in crypto
Because the move that follows is usually small
u20l5-5.explanation: It often gets the direction right, but the move is short. It's also very common (rank 11).

u20l5-6.prompt: Candle 1, red: opens at €30 and closes at €27. Candle 2, green: opens at €26.50. Above what price does it need to close to be a bullish engulfing?
u20l5-6.explanation: It has to close above the red candle's open (€30), so that its body covers the whole red one.

u20l5-7.prompt: In dark cloud cover, the red candle closes below the ____ of the previous green body.
u20l5-7.explanation: If it engulfed it completely, it would be a bearish engulfing.

u20l5-8.prompt: Patterns with gaps between candles mean the same in crypto as in shares.
u20l5-8.explanation: Crypto trades 24/7 and forex almost non-stop: there are hardly any gaps between candles, so these patterns form differently or lose their meaning.

u20l5-9.prompt: Quick: a green candle whose body swallows the previous red body, after a fall.

u20l5-10.prompt: Marta finds a textbook bearish engulfing. She knows it reverses 79 % of the time and wants to bet big. What has she forgotten to check?
options: The colour of the previous candle
How far it could fall compared with what she loses if it fails
u20l5-10.explanation: Getting the direction right isn't enough: you have to compare the expected move with the risk.
feedback: She already knows: green. The important question is how much she gains if she's right and how much she loses if it fails.
It often gets the direction right, but if the move is small and the stop is big, she can lose money while being right.
Exactly: with a small average move, the reward/risk ratio may not be worth it.

u20l6-1.prompt: Put the candles of a morning star in order.
options: Long red candle after a fall
Long green candle that closes above the midpoint of the first
u20l6-1.explanation: Sellers dominate, then hesitate, and finally buyers take control.

u20l6-2.prompt: Tap the candle that completes the morning star.
u20l6-2.explanation: After a long red candle and a small candle of doubt, this long green one completes the pattern. (Amazon · daily candles · July–August 2025)

Because they only exist in Japan

u20l7-1.prompt: What are the four filters that give a candlestick pattern value? Tick all that apply.
u20l7-1.explanation: Without them, the pattern is little more than noise. And on minute charts, noise rules.

u20l7-2.prompt: Challenge: look only at the candles and decide. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u20l7-2.explanation: Keep track of your hits in these challenges: with enough attempts you'll see that, using candles alone, they're about the same as tossing a coin.

u20l7-3.prompt: Different asset, another go. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u20l7-3.explanation: Every chart has its own story, but none comes with the answer written on it. What you do control is how much you risk.

u20l7-4.prompt: And one more. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u20l7-4.explanation: Three attempts are far too few to draw conclusions: that's why serious studies use thousands of cases.

u20l7-5.prompt: If a pattern gets the direction right 60 % of the time, it's bound to be profitable.
u20l7-5.explanation: It depends on the size of the move when it's right, what you lose when it's wrong, and costs.

u20l7-6.prompt: Marshall, Young and Rose concluded that 28 candlestick patterns added no value on Dow Jones shares.
u20l7-6.explanation: And a study of the Japanese market (1975–2004) came to the same conclusion.

u20l7-7.prompt: You see a shooting star on a crypto's 5-minute chart, in the middle of a range and on low volume. How many filters does it meet?
u20l7-7.explanation: There's no prior trend, no relevant level, volume is low and there's no confirmation. On top of that, on a 5-minute chart noise rules.

options: Looking at data in real time
Testing lots of patterns until one seems to work by pure chance
u20l7-8.explanation: Run enough tests and chance will always hand you some «discovery».

u20l7-9.prompt: A share in a year-long uptrend pulls back 12 % to its 200-session moving average, which coincides with an old high. It forms a hammer on high volume and the next day closes above it. Bruno sees all four filters. What's the sensible thing to do?
options: Never go in: candlesticks don't work
Go in without a stop: with four out of four it can't fail
If he goes in, a stop below the hammer's low and a small position
u20l7-9.explanation: Context improves the odds; the stop and the position size protect you when it still goes wrong.
feedback: Candles on their own add little, but with context they're a reasonable clue for someone trading with a plan.
It can still fail. Without a stop, one failure can cost far more than expected.
Exactly: four out of four improves the odds, and risk management protects him when it fails.

u20l7-10.prompt: A candlestick pattern on a daily chart is more meaningful than on a 1-minute chart.

u20l7-11.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: It depends on how many followers they have
